title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify system function and distinguish context from quantitative evidence.
student: What is the primary structural function of the suspended platform system shown in the industry image?
instructor: The system supports workers, equipment, or other loads at an elevated position and transfers their weight through the suspension members to an overhead lifting or supporting system. The photograph supplies physical context, not the numerical model or an operating-load rating.

title: External Loading
learningObjectives: Identify real loads and distinguish them from a later idealized load case.
student: What external loads would normally act on a suspended work platform during use or lifting?
instructor: A real system carries the weights of its platforms, workers, tools and equipment and may also experience dynamic, wind or other environmental loads. Load position can produce unequal suspension forces. The quantitative phase will explicitly prescribe its load case and omitted effects; real-system loads must not be silently assumed included in that prescription.

title: Supports and Restraints
learningObjectives: Recognize tension-only behavior and the limits of the modeled restraints.
student: How is the platform supported, and what type of forces can the suspension members transmit?
instructor: Suspension members connect the platform to an overhead lifting or support system and carry tension. Ideal flexible members do not carry compression or end moments; a slack member supplies no tensile restraint until it becomes taut. A vertical-only model does not by itself establish lateral or out-of-plane stability.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace load transfer without bypassing intermediate structural members.
student: Trace the dominant load path from the supported load to the overhead lifting or supporting system.
instructor: The load passes from the payload into the platform, through the suspension members, and into the overhead supporting structure. A two-level model must also account for load transmitted into and through the intermediate member before reaching the ceiling.

title: Effect of Load Position
learningObjectives: Predict qualitative effects of load position without claiming universal improvement.
student: What would you expect to happen if the supported load is positioned closer to one side of the platform rather than near its center?
instructor: Suspension members would generally carry unequal tensile forces. With comparable member stiffnesses, unequal forces produce unequal extensions and can change platform orientation. A multi-level system can respond differently at its different levels; moving a load toward one member's center is not a general guarantee of smaller motion everywhere.

title: Relevant Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Distinguish axial extension, translation and rotation.
student: If the engineering concern is the position and orientation of the platform after loading, what mechanical responses must be considered?
instructor: Consider extension of the suspension members, absolute vertical movement of the connected points, and rotation of each platform or rigid member. A member's relative axial extension is different from the absolute movement of its lower attachment when its upper attachment also moves.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify physical parameters before adopting a particular common model.
student: What loading, geometric, and material characteristics would you expect to influence the displacement and tilt of the suspended system?
instructor: Relevant characteristics include load magnitude and position; suspension lengths, cross-sectional areas and material or assembly axial stiffness; suspension-point spacing and connectivity; support flexibility; and whether deformation remains within the selected model's assumptions. At this context stage, identify physical dependencies rather than guessing the later common model's symbols.
gradingNotes: Assess physical dependencies without requiring students to guess the common model's symbols or exact geometry.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Develop an independent idealization before using a supplied quantitative model.
student: Convert the real suspended-platform system into a simplified Mechanics of Materials model that preserves the platform, tensile suspension members, overhead supports, load location, suspension-point spacing, and the possibility of vertical displacement and rotation. Draw and label your own model and state what physical features it retains. A common model will be supplied after Q10 for the quantitative phase.
instructor: A suitable independent model represents load-carrying platforms or members connected to overhead support by deformable tension members, with clear attachment points, load location and possible translation/rotation. Other defensible models are acceptable when their load path and assumptions are consistent. Grade this task for reasoning and a usable idealization, not for guessing the later common model's exact labels. Do not give students a completed free-body diagram in this question.
gradingNotes: Grade the independent model for physical consistency and explicit assumptions. Do not require exact agreement with the later common-model labels. No completed instructor free body is supplied before this task.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions and distinguish an exclusion from a demonstrated negligible effect.
student: State and justify the assumptions used in your simplified model. Identify at least two real effects that your model omits.
instructor: Reasonable stated assumptions may include quasi-static loading, rigid platform members, linearly elastic axial suspension members, small deformation and rotation, idealized connections, and sufficiently stiff overhead support. Omitting self-weight, member bending, assembly/termination compliance, sag, dynamics or lateral motion must be identified as a modeling assumption, not proof that the effect is negligible. The common-model panel after Q10 specifies the assumptions used for the numerical work.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan equilibrium, deformation, compatibility and model checks in a defensible sequence.
student: Before calculating, describe the analysis sequence required to determine vertical displacement and tilt.
instructor: Check the common geometry, input units and model admissibility; draw separate free bodies; solve equilibrium for the tensile forces; calculate axial extensions with consistent units; combine support motion and relative extension using rigid-body compatibility; calculate load-point movement and signed rotations; then assess weighted displacement contributions and a scoped engineering change. Retain unrounded values until final display.

title: Common-Model Boundary Conditions and Unknown Wire Forces
learningObjectives: Read the supplied geometry and identify tension-only force transfer and boundary conditions.
student: Using the unsolved common-model geometry and assumptions supplied after Q10, identify the fixed points, the two rigid members, the four unknown wire tensions, and the load path. Explain what the eye connections do and do not restrain.
instructor: E and F have fixed coordinates. DC and AB are rigid members. The unknown tensile forces are TED, TFC, TAH and TBC along their initially vertical wires. AH connects H to endpoint A, and BC connects C to endpoint B. The load path is P → AB → AH/BC → DC → ED/FC → E/F. Eye connections transmit the modeled axial forces without applied end couples; fixed ceiling points do not make the rigid members clamped. All four wires must remain taut for this selected model.

title: Equilibrium of Lower Rigid Member AB
learningObjectives: Determine lower-wire tensions from a correct endpoint-supported free body.
student: Draw the free-body diagram of lower member AB and solve for the forces in the lower wires AH and BC. State your force and moment sign conventions.
instructor: Take upward forces and counterclockwise moments as positive. On AB, TAH acts upward at A, TBC upward at B, and P downward at xP from A. ΣF_y = TAH + TBC − P = 0 and ΣM_A = TBC LAB − P xP = 0. Thus TBC = P xP/LAB = {{P}}({{x_P}})/{{L_AB}} = {{platform_T_BC_lb}} lbf, and TAH = P − TBC = {{platform_T_AH_lb}} lbf. Use unrounded forces in subsequent calculations.
gradingNotes: Use the agreed endpoint-supported AB geometry. Show tension at A and B and a downward interior P; carry unrounded values into later work. A compressive reaction is not admissible for a suspension wire.

title: Equilibrium of Upper Rigid Member DC
learningObjectives: Transfer equal/opposite lower-wire forces and verify local and global equilibrium.
student: Draw the free-body diagram of upper member DC and solve for the forces in the upper wires ED and FC. Show both forces applied at C and verify equilibrium of the whole assembly.
instructor: The lower wires apply downward TAH at H and downward TBC at C. The upper wires apply upward TED at D and upward TFC at C; the two C forces are at the same node. ΣF_y = TED + TFC − TAH − TBC = 0. ΣM_D = TFC LDC − TAH xDH − TBC LDC = 0. Therefore TFC = (TAH xDH + TBC LDC)/LDC = {{platform_T_FC_lb}} lbf and TED = P − TFC = {{platform_T_ED_lb}} lbf. The whole assembly satisfies TED + TFC = P and TFC LDC = P(xDH + xP), using geometric closure. Ceiling loads are opposite to the upward reactions on the assembly.

title: Wire Elongations
learningObjectives: Calculate four relative axial extensions with consistent force, length and modulus units.
student: Calculate the elongation of each wire using δ = T L/(A E). Use consistent inch–pound-force units and state which material/member assumptions this equation requires.
instructor: Use Epsi = 1000 Ew = {{platform_E_w_psi}} lbf/in², Aw = {{A_w}} in², Lu,in = 12 Lu = {{platform_L_u_in}} in, and Ll,in = 12 Ll = {{platform_L_l_in}} in. For constant area and the assigned linear axial stiffness, δAH = TAH Ll,in/(Aw Epsi) = {{platform_delta_AH_in}} in; δBC = {{platform_delta_BC_in}} in; δED = TED Lu,in/(Aw Epsi) = {{platform_delta_ED_in}} in; δFC = {{platform_delta_FC_in}} in. These are relative wire extensions. The assigned A/E model is not a verified rope/chain stiffness or a strength check.

title: Displacement of Point H on Upper Member DC
learningObjectives: Interpolate rigid-body motion at an intermediate attachment point.
student: Using rigid-body compatibility of upper member DC and downward-positive displacement, determine the vertical displacement of point H.
instructor: The fixed upper anchors give vD = δED and vC = δFC. Let h = xDH/LDC. Then vH = (1−h)vD + h vC = δED + (δFC−δED)(xDH/LDC) = {{platform_delta_H_in}} in downward. The interpolation uses the undeformed attachment coordinates and the first-order rigid-member model.

title: Displacement of Endpoints A and B of Lower Member AB
learningObjectives: Combine support motion and relative extension without treating the lower-wire tops as fixed.
student: Determine the downward displacement of points A and B. Account for movement of the upper ends of both lower wires.
instructor: A is vertically below H and B is vertically below C. Therefore vA = vH + δAH = {{platform_delta_A_in}} in downward and vB = vC + δBC = {{platform_delta_B_in}} in downward. The upper attachment points are not fixed. These sums use unrounded internal quantities; displayed component values may be rounded.

title: Vertical Displacement of the Load
learningObjectives: Interpolate load-point motion from lower-member endpoint movements.
student: Determine the vertical displacement of the load point on lower member AB using its undeformed location.
instructor: Let r = xP/LAB. The rigid-member displacement is affine, so vP = (1−r)vA + r vB = vA + (vB−vA)(xP/LAB) = {{platform_delta_load_in}} in downward. This is load-point movement from the stipulated initial reference state.

title: Signed Tilt of Lower Member AB
learningObjectives: Report a signed rotation, magnitude and result-dependent direction including a level case.
student: Determine the signed small-angle rotation and tilt magnitude of AB. Use downward-positive displacement and clockwise-positive rotation, and identify the direction or state that the member remains level.
instructor: Δv_AB = vB−vA = {{platform_delta_B_minus_A_in}} in. With LAB,in = {{platform_L_AB_in}} in, θAB ≈ Δv_AB/LAB,in = {{platform_theta_AB_signed_rad}} rad = {{platform_theta_AB_signed_deg}}°. Its magnitude is {{platform_theta_AB_rad}} rad = {{platform_theta_AB_deg}}°. {{platform_lower_tilt_explanation}} Use unrounded displacement differences; the stated zero/tie tolerance is numerical, not a physical levelness criterion.

title: Signed Tilt of Upper Member DC
learningObjectives: Interpret upper-member signed rotation consistently, including zero and reversed tilt.
student: Determine the signed small-angle rotation and tilt magnitude of DC using the same sign convention. Identify the direction or state that the member remains level.
instructor: Δv_DC = vC−vD = δFC−δED = {{platform_delta_C_minus_D_in}} in. With LDC,in = {{platform_L_DC_in}} in, θDC ≈ Δv_DC/LDC,in = {{platform_theta_DC_signed_rad}} rad = {{platform_theta_DC_signed_deg}}°. Its magnitude is {{platform_theta_DC_rad}} rad = {{platform_theta_DC_deg}}°. {{platform_upper_tilt_explanation}} Use unrounded differences and do not infer a tilt direction from a rounded zero.

title: Weighted Contributions to Load-Point Displacement
learningObjectives: Derive compatibility weights and rank the contributions to one specified response.
student: Using the compatibility equations, express vP as a weighted sum of the four wire elongations. Calculate each wire's contribution to vP and identify the largest contribution, including any tie. Explain why the largest wire elongation need not make the largest contribution to load-point movement.
instructor: Let r = xP/LAB and h = xDH/LDC. Substitution gives vP = (1−r)δAH + rδBC + (1−r)(1−h)δED + [h+r(1−h)]δFC. Thus wAH = {{platform_weight_AH}}, wBC = {{platform_weight_BC}}, wED = {{platform_weight_ED}}, and wFC = {{platform_weight_FC}}. With ci = wi δi, the contributions are AH: {{platform_contrib_AH_in}} in ({{platform_contrib_AH_percent}}%); BC: {{platform_contrib_BC_in}} in ({{platform_contrib_BC_percent}}%); ED: {{platform_contrib_ED_in}} in ({{platform_contrib_ED_percent}}%); FC: {{platform_contrib_FC_in}} in ({{platform_contrib_FC_percent}}%). Their sum is {{platform_contribution_sum_in}} in, agreeing with vP before rounding. {{platform_dominant_summary}} {{platform_largest_elongation_summary}} A wire's raw extension and its weighted contribution are different response measures.

title: Scoped Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Make a parameter-dependent recommendation supported by the specified response and explicit limits.
student: Summarize the predicted load-point displacement and both signed rotations with directions. Identify the maximum wire tension and the largest weighted contribution to load-point displacement, including ties. Recommend one change, stating what remains fixed and what must be rechecked. Explain why these results alone do not approve a real platform for service.
instructor: The load point moves {{platform_delta_load_in}} in downward. θAB = {{platform_theta_AB_signed_rad}} rad; direction: {{platform_lower_tilt_direction}}. θDC = {{platform_theta_DC_signed_rad}} rad; direction: {{platform_upper_tilt_direction}}. {{platform_force_max_summary}} {{platform_dominant_summary}} At fixed load position and geometry, uniformly increasing the common Aw or Ew, or reducing P, scales down this linear model's displacement and rotation magnitudes without changing the geometry weights. Uniformly scaling all four free lengths also requires a consistent new vertical geometry. Relocating P or changing only one wire group requires recalculating vP and both rotations; moving P toward AB's center is not a universal improvement. No material/assembly provenance, strength allowable, connector capacity, displacement/tilt service limit, real-platform bending response or full stability assessment is established. {{platform_model_status_note}}
gradingNotes: Judge the recommendation against the stated response and what is held fixed. Require recalculation for load relocation or selective stiffness changes. Strength, real assembly behavior, connector capacity and complete service acceptance are not established by these data.
